mcqs.question: In a layered abuse-defense pipeline, why do cheap, coarse checks (IP reputation, request rate) run before expensive, accurate ones (device fingerprinting, behavioral signals)?
options: Coarse checks filter out most bad traffic cheaply, so expensive checks only run on the smaller set of requests that need them
Expensive checks are always less accurate than coarse ones
Regulations require rate limiting to run before any other security check
Device fingerprinting cannot run unless IP reputation has already passed for unrelated technical reasons
mcqs.explanation: Ordering cheap-and-coarse before expensive-and-accurate means you don't pay the cost of deep checks on traffic that coarse signals already reject — it's a cost-efficiency design, not a regulatory or technical dependency requirement, and expensive checks are typically more accurate, not less.

mcqs.question: Why does placing the abuse-signal check before the core business logic matter, rather than after?
options: It has no real effect on system load either way
It protects the expensive parts of the system — the database, downstream services — from ever seeing rejected traffic
It makes the abuse check itself run faster
Core business logic cannot include any validation of its own
mcqs.explanation: Checking before the core path means abusive requests are rejected before they consume the resources they were targeting — the database, payment processing, message queues. It doesn't change the check's own speed, and it doesn't mean business logic skips its own validation; the two are complementary.

mcqs.question: What's the concrete test for whether an audit trail was actually designed rather than accumulated from debug logs?
options: Whether logs exist somewhere in the system at all
Whether the logs are stored in JSON format
Whether you can answer 'who deleted this specific row, and when' in seconds, not by reconstructing intent from scattered application logs
Whether every microservice has its own separate logging library
mcqs.explanation: A designed audit trail answers a specific, sensitive-action question fast and directly — the format of the logs and whether every service has its own library are irrelevant if the actual question can't be answered quickly. Logs existing somewhere isn't the same as an audit trail existing.

mcqs.question: A signal is ambiguous — unusual login timing that could be a legitimate user traveling, or could be account takeover. What's the better response?
options: Block the login attempt in real time immediately
Ignore the signal entirely since it isn't conclusive
Permanently ban the account without further review
Flag it for async review or step-up verification rather than an immediate hard block
mcqs.explanation: Ambiguous signals belong in async review or a lighter-weight step-up challenge, since a hard real-time block on a weak signal risks locking out a legitimate user with high confidence in a low-confidence situation. Ignoring it or banning outright are both extremes that ignore the actual confidence level of the signal.

mcqs.question: A team says 'we log everything, so we have an audit trail,' but an incident review takes an afternoon of grepping across six services' debug logs. What does this reveal?
options: Debug logging and a designed audit trail are not the same thing — sensitive actions need a dedicated, indexed, long-retention record
The team needs more storage capacity for their logs
The incident itself was handled correctly and no change is needed
Audit trails are unnecessary if logs exist anywhere in the system
mcqs.explanation: General debug logs — scattered, short-retention, mixed with operational noise — are not a substitute for a purpose-built audit trail of sensitive actions. Needing an afternoon to answer a basic question is exactly the symptom described, not something storage capacity fixes, and it clearly does need a change.
